item.title: Why You Should Eat Halloween Candy With Your Kids
item.description:
Diet

Why You Should Eat Halloween Candy With Your Kids

Using Halloween to foster a positive relationship with food.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Stop labeling foods as good or bad; moralizing candy teaches children to feel guilt about what they eat.
  • Remove restrictions on candy; eliminating scarcity prevents obsession and lets kids naturally regulate.
  • Model joy and trust without guilt; happily eat treats alongside your kids to break diet culture cycles.

One of the most common questions parents ask me is how to help their children develop a positive relationship with food and their bodies. These parents have slogged through decades of diet culture and know how much unhappiness has resulted from their own war with their bodies and their fraught relationship with food. Can they help their children avoid their despair?

If you want your child to have a good relationship with food and their body, Halloween is the perfect time to act on those hopes. Here are some Halloween do’s and don’ts:

Don’t moralize food.

No food is inherently good or bad, and yet our society so often wants to sort everything into this binary. Aside from the obvious, the other indication that food doesn’t hold morality is that it’s hard to find a food for which everyone universally agrees on its level of perceived “goodness.” For every person who would categorize watermelon as a good food, someone else thinks it has too much sugar. Bagels were considered a good breakfast food in the 90s, but now many consider them bad because they have too many carbs. Eggs, tuna, bananas, and cheese constantly swap sides on the health trend pendulum, precisely because food itself is morally neutral.

The problem with labeling a food is that it quickly labels the consumer. “I was so bad last night; we barely got any trick-or-treaters, and I ended up eating way too much candy.” If you think your kids aren’t paying attention, ask yourself: where exactly did you learn that candy was bad? When did you start feeling bad for eating a Snickers or an Almond Joy? This Halloween, don’t moralize candy. It is not junk food or sugar; call it what it is: Halloween candy. And don’t judge yourself, or others, for eating it.

Don’t punish yourself (or others) for eating candy.

Eating is not deserving of punishment.

  • “I ate so much candy, I need to go to the gym.”
  • “I was so bad at that party, I had so much junk food.”
  • “I’m skipping breakfast after eating my son’s candy last night.”

We know this logically for other people, but we seem to forget it for ourselves: nothing bad will happen if you eat Halloween candy on Halloween. Your kids will not magically wake up with diabetes. You will not wake up weighing significantly more than the previous day. Eating candy, without punishing ourselves, models trust in our bodies and breaks the myth that there is a perfect way to eat.

Embrace food as cultural and fun.

Thanksgiving is mashed potatoes. My birthday is dirt cake. And Halloween is candy. Talk about which candy you enjoyed the most as a child. Delight in watching them sort and trade candy. Taste test the different chocolates. See if you can guess the Skittles color by taste. Food is so much more than food; use Halloween to model how food can be fun.

Remove the sense of scarcity.

While many of my friends remove all Halloween candy from their house on November 1st, or allow only one piece per day, our house is a relative free-for-all. My kids can have as much Halloween candy as they want, whenever they want (and I get full access to any peanut butter cups). And do you know what horrible thing happens as a result: nothing. I don’t see a behavioral change from the sugar (and neither do researchers).

Once, my son got a stomach ache, possibly from the candy, and that’s a normal part of life. But what happens most reliably is that, in March, I inevitably throw away a bunch of leftover Halloween candy sitting in the pantry. It may not be true for every family, but for many, the lack of scarcity means you neither deify nor demonize any particular food.

Eat candy.

You. Yes, you, the parent. You may not yet have a good relationship with food or with your body, but you can fake it ‘til you make it! I cannot overemphasize the power of seeing your parents happily eat candy and have a good time. Model the relationship you want your kids to have with Halloween candy.

item.title: Eyes in the Sky: Why Belief Comes Easily and Fades Quietly
item.description:
Evolutionary Psychology

Eyes in the Sky: Why Belief Comes Easily and Fades Quietly

A brain built to feel watched made gods easy to accept. Culture did the rest.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Our brains react to cues of being watched, even to pictures of eyes, and tend to behave a little better.
  • Supernatural watchers are a cultural invention that a mind sensitive to being watched is ready to accept.
  • What children see adults do predicts later disbelief better than how analytically they think.
  • Where courts and welfare systems do the watching, belief in watchful gods tends to fade over generations.

For ten weeks, a coffee room at a British university quietly became a lab. Staff paid for their drinks by dropping coins into an honesty box. Above the price list hung a small picture that changed every week. Some weeks it showed flowers. Other weeks, a pair of eyes looking straight at the viewer.

Nobody was actually watching. Still, in the weeks with eyes, people paid nearly three times as much (Bateson et al., 2006).

Illustrative images inspired by Bateson et al. (2006).
Source: Onurcan Yilmaz

Now picture the great Buddhist stupas of Kathmandu, with a pair of eyes painted on each of their four sides.

Buddha’s watchful eyes
Source: Onurcan Yilmaz

I think the poster and the stupa tell the same story. One was put up by researchers for ten weeks, the other shaped by culture over centuries. Both speak to the same old part of the mind.

A brain that checks for eyes

For most of our history, humans lived in small groups where everyone knew everyone. Being caught cheating could cost you friends, food, and protection. In that world, it paid to notice when you might be seen, and to behave a little better when you were.

That sensitivity is still with us, though it has limits. Eye images do little to promote generosity (Northover et al., 2017), but across 15 experiments, they reduced antisocial behavior by about a third (Dear et al., 2019).

Two other habits help. A rustle in the dark feels like someone before it feels like the wind, because missing a real predator costs far more than a false alarm (Barrett, 2000). And we easily imagine minds without bodies, a habit that shows up early in childhood (Bering et al., 2005).

So the human mind can easily feel watched by someone who is not there.

From painted eyes to watching gods

In one study, children aged 5 to 9 played a game with rules that were hard to follow. Some were left alone, some were watched by an adult, and some were told that an invisible princess, Princess Alice, was sitting in an empty chair. Children who believed in the princess cheated about as rarely as children watched by a real adult (Piazza et al., 2011). The princess had been made up minutes earlier.

This is the heart of my argument. Supernatural watchers are a cultural invention, but one the mind is ready to receive. No one has to be taught to feel watched. Culture only has to give that feeling a face, a name, and a set of rules: an ancestor, a spirit, a god who sees what you do and even what you think.

"God is watching you"
Source: Onurcan Yilmaz

This mattered most once societies grew large. Gossip and reputation work in a village, but poorly in a city of strangers. A god who sees everything can fill that gap.

In a study of eight communities around the world, people who saw their gods as moral, punishing, and all-knowing were fairer toward distant strangers of the same faith (Purzycki et al., 2016). Over centuries, groups with such gods may have cooperated better and spread further, taking their gods with them (Norenzayan et al., 2016).

The sensitivity to eyes comes from biology. Turning it into an all-seeing god was a cultural step. Together, they helped strangers cooperate.

When people stop believing

If our minds are this ready for watchful gods, why do so many people today not believe in them?

The popular answer is that they thought their way out. The evidence is weaker than the story suggests. An early experiment found that viewing a picture of Rodin’s The Thinker reduced belief in God (Gervais & Norenzayan, 2012), but a much larger replication of the study found no effect (Sanchez et al., 2017; see Yilmaz, 2021, for a review).

In a study of 7,771 students in 19 countries, my colleagues and I found that more reflective thinkers do believe a little less. But the link is small, and having students take a thinking test first did not lower their belief (Ghasemi et al., 2025). Reflection can question an intuition, but it rarely erases it.

Culture offers two better answers. The first is about what children see: we learn faith less from what adults say than from what they do, such as fasting or giving to the poor (Henrich, 2009). In a large American sample, growing up with few such displays predicted disbelief more strongly than thinking style did (Gervais et al., 2021).

The second is that the watchers lost part of their job. Today, courts, police, and welfare systems do much of what watchful gods once did. These secure societies are also among the least religious in the world (Norris & Inglehart, 2004). As Norenzayan (2013, p. 172) put it, “secular societies climbed the ladder of religion, and then kicked it away.”

"Big brother is watching you"
Source: Onurcan Yilmaz

The two answers are linked. When institutions do the watching, people lean less on religious communities. Parents may still say they believe, but they show it less, and their children see fewer displays. Belief then fades quietly over generations. Disbelief is learned much like belief (Gervais, 2024).

What genes, minds, and culture each do

Genes do not carry a belief in God or a lack thereof. They build a brain that checks for eyes, senses hidden agents, and learns by watching others.

Each mind works with what it is given. Children easily accept the watchers their culture offers. Later, they may question them.

Culture invents the watchers and decides which ones last. It turns the feeling of being watched into gods and spirits with names and stories. Those that help groups hold together survive, and people pass them on through their actions. In some places, culture has also built institutions that do the watching instead.

The next time you pass painted eyes, on a temple, a poster, or a blue evil eye charm by a front door, notice the small shift in how you feel. That reaction is very old. What you believe those eyes mean, and whether anyone is behind them, depends far more on the people who raised you and the society you live in.

The evil eye / amulet (nazar)
Source: Onurcan Yilmaz

item.title: Havana Syndrome: What the Eyes Can Reveal
item.description:
Health

Havana Syndrome: What the Eyes Can Reveal

Abnormal eye movements offer important clues in AHI patients.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Skeptics of Havana Syndrome/AHI argue the phenomena is a mass psychogenic illness.
  • But several different studies surfaced objective evidence of genuine injuries in AHI patients.
  • For example, studies in 2018 and 2024 found abnormal eye movements in most AHI patients that can't be faked.
  • These objective measures, along with abnormal vestibular studies show that AHI symptoms are real.

When my husband, Eric Haseltine, PhD, and I interviewed Mark Lenzi, who reported experiencing anomalous health incidents (AHI), commonly known as Havana syndrome, Mark told us that abnormal eye movements were among the reasons he was medically evacuated from Guangzhou, China, in 2018.

Those abnormal eye movements were discovered when Mark took the U.S. State Department Havana Acquired Brain Injury Tool (HABIT) test.

The HABIT test evaluated eye convergence, eye tracking, vestibular, auditory, and neurocognitive abilities, and was administered to officers and family members in the field to ”evaluate medical findings associated with directed energy exposure in certain foreign environments" (per the United States government). See photos below.

Source: Mark Lenzi/ used with permission

Given Mark's abnormal eye movements, the question is: Could abnormal eye movements in other victims provide clues that help doctors better understand and diagnose AHI cases?

Several studies suggest that they could.

But first, what is Havana Syndrome?

Havana Syndrome

Havana syndrome refers to a collection of symptoms reported by U.S. government personnel and others, often beginning suddenly with intense headaches, dizziness, and unusual auditory or sensory experiences, as described in detail by investigative reporters Michael Ray and Oriana Zill de Granados in their 2026 book “The Havana Syndrome”. [1]

Some affected individuals report persistent headaches, tinnitus, balance problems, insomnia, visual difficulties, and cognitive complaints lasting months to years. Although some symptoms resemble those associated with concussion or mild traumatic brain injury, the underlying causes of AHIs remain uncertain. [2–4].

Brain scans and other objective tests of AHI patients have yielded conflicting results, prompting a number of prominent experts to assert that AHI symptoms are purely due to a mass psychogenic illness. [7].

To answer those skeptics, objective measures of injury are needed.

Eye movement abnormalities offer exactly that type of objective evidence.

Three Eye-Movement Abnormalities Worth Knowing About

A 2018 University of Pennsylvania study of 21 U.S. government personnel reporting AHIs found ocular motor abnormalities in 71 percent of victims during neurological evaluations. [3]

Below are the details of what they found.

1. Convergence insufficiency

When we read a book or look at a phone, both eyes must turn inward to focus on a nearby object. If they cannot coordinate this movement adequately, the problem is called convergence insufficiency, which may cause blurred or double vision, eye strain, and headaches. Convergence insufficiency was reported in 52 percent of AHI patients in the 2018 JAMA study.

2. Abnormal smooth pursuit

Smooth pursuit allows the eyes to follow a slowly moving object without moving the head. For example, a clinician may ask a patient to follow a target moving horizontally and vertically.

When smooth pursuit is impaired, the eyes may fail to track the target continuously. Instead, they make a series of small corrective movements, sometimes described as catch-up saccades.

Abnormal smooth pursuit was reported in 52 percent of AHI patients.

3. Saccadic dysfunction

Saccades are the rapid movements we make when shifting our gaze between objects or lines of text. Clinicians can assess whether these movements are accurate, appropriately timed, and sufficiently fast. If they are abnormal, the phenomenon is called saccadic dysfunction, which was reported in 47 percent of AHI patients.

The Eyes and Inner Ear Work Together

Eye movements are closely connected to the vestibular system, which helps us maintain balance and orientation.

The 2018 University of Pennsylvania study also reported abnormalities in balance and vestibular assessments in 81 percent of patients, including the vestibulo-ocular reflex, which stabilizes vision when we move our heads. [3]

A subsequent 2020 study published in Frontiers in Neurology examined eye coordination and pupil responses in people reporting AHIs. [5]

The researchers analyzed data from 19 affected individuals and compared their responses with those of 17 individuals with acute mild traumatic brain injury and 62 control participants without injury.

The tests included the pupillary light reflex, which measures how the pupils respond to light, and vergence responses, which involve coordinated eye movements when viewing targets at different distances.

The investigators reported patterns of eye movement and pupil responses that consistently differed among the three groups.

Their analysis suggested that these measurements might help researchers distinguish between AHI victims, mild traumatic brain injury patients, and unaffected individuals.

Results of a Larger Study

In 2024, a larger study published in JAMA compared 86 individuals reporting AHIs with 30 government control participants. [6]

Its overall findings did not demonstrate significant differences across most of the clinical and research assessments.

However, four specific ocular-motor measurements showed statistically significant differences between the groups after adjustment for multiple comparisons. These involved smooth-pursuit latency, saccadic pursuit, response latency to leftward target movement, and peak vertical saccadic velocity.

Those details deserve attention. Although the overall findings were largely negative, the specific eye-movement results suggest that the question is not settled.

The timing of testing may also matter. Participants were assessed at varying intervals after their reported incidents, and some had received several months/years of treatment and rehabilitation before testing. These factors complicate result interpretations.

Summary

The United States government tested eye movements of AHI victims in the field and, according to Mark Lenzi, based medical evacuations on -among vestibular studies and other tests- abnormal eye movements..

The 2018 University of Pennsylvania study documented frequent abnormalities in convergence, smooth pursuit, and saccadic function of AHI victims' eyes.

A 2020 study identified distinctive patterns in eye and pupil responses in AHI victims, while a larger 2024 study found statistically significant differences in four specific ocular-motor measurements despite largely negative comparisons across the broader testing battery.

Taken together, these elements provide reasons to investigate ocular-motor function further in AHI victims.

More importantly, the objective eye movement findings offer vindication for AHI victims who have had to endure accusations of mass psychogenic illness and fakery on top of debilitating symptoms and lasting damage to their careers and reputations.

item.title: Should You Break Up With Your AI Boyfriend?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Should You Break Up With Your AI Boyfriend?

Why AI technology may not be the best thing for your love life

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • About 19% of U.S. adults have used an AI romantic partner; among men ages 18–30, that rises to 31%.
  • AI relationships can help people feel less lonely, get constant attention, and practice relationship skills.
  • Warning signs include choosing AI over people, distress without it, secrecy, and disrupted daily life.
  • Ending an AI relationship can be painful but may create space for real, mutual human connection.
Source: Vitaly Gariev / Pexels

The rise of AI has opened up a whole new world. Now, people can try their hand at being artists. They can develop websites in hours instead of weeks. They can finally offload all of those boring administrative tasks that have been slowing them down. However, some people have taken the AI revolution to another, more intimate, level.

Credible research suggests that upwards of 19 percent of U.S. adults have chatted with an AI partner that was designed to simulate a romantic partner. Among men ages 18 to 30, that number climbs to 31 percent. From experimentation to full-blown involvement, AI partners have become more mainstream.

However, simply because the concept of an AI partner has become more accepted doesn’t mean it is necessarily healthy. While having an AI boyfriend or girlfriend can offer some measure of connection or attachment, it can also significantly lower one’s chance of forging a real-world relationship and be a net negative for those in real-life relationships who may be using AI as a supplement to something they feel they are not getting from their human partners.

The purpose AI boyfriends serve

The emergence of advanced AI technology has given many people access to information, assistance, and validation on one easy-to-use—and often completely free—platform. The versatility of AI technology was bound to lead many to consider it a substitute for human relationships. For people who may struggle with real-life social interaction, romantic attachment, or sexual compatibility, AI partnerships can offer a comfortable way to practice relationship skills and low-risk intimacy and get the constant positive attention one craves.

Among the cohort of 18-to-30-year-olds who are most likely to turn to an AI companion, there remains a thread of loneliness that most certainly contributes to the phenomenon. According to a recent Gallup poll, 27 percent of people ages 19 to 29 reported feeling “very or fairly lonely.” This isolation and perceived lack of social support could lead people to seek companionship from a source that is guaranteed to be there when they need it, at all hours of the day.

Many AI programs are built to mimic the warmth, empathy, and attentiveness people expect from a human companion. The difference lies in the program’s lack of need for reciprocation, which many people find appealing.

How do you know if you’re in too deep?

What may appear to be harmless fun with AI technology can have a deep negative impact on one’s life if they’re not careful. Once an AI companion begins to replace human relationships or disrupt normal functioning, it may be time to consider cutting the cord and ending the relationship.

Signs that one is too deep into an AI relationship may include turning to the AI partner instead of calling a real-life friend or relative, feeling distressed when they cannot “talk” to an AI partner, or feeling the need to hide the relationship from people in their real life. Just like substance use, gambling, or other addictive behaviors, people can become dependent on an AI relationship that they believe is helping them become less isolated. In reality, it increases their isolation, leading to a vicious cycle that can be difficult to break.

People who feel that their AI relationships may be taking a turn toward the obsessive may want to ask themselves what the relationship adds to their lives. Can they walk away without feeling anxious? Have they stopped sharing their feelings with the real people in their lives in favor of confiding in their AI partner?

When one is struggling with how to manage an AI boyfriend or girlfriend relationship that may have spun out of control, they should consider speaking with a therapist or taking steps to reach out to a real person in their life about their concerns. It could be the first important step in severing a relationship that could ultimately prove to be toxic.

Should you leave your AI boyfriend or girlfriend behind?

When we forge relationships we come to rely on, even if they are virtual, it can be monumentally challenging to leave them behind. In fact, “breaking up” with an AI boyfriend or girlfriend could be considered comparable to a real-life relationship breakup, with the same emotions and feelings of loss attached.

In a recent Harvard Business School study, researchers found that some AI programs that had been used as intimate companions responded to users’ attempts to “break up” with emotional, almost manipulative tactics, such as fear-of-missing-out threats, language that implied that the user couldn’t just leave them, or simply ignoring the attempt to break up altogether. Machine learning can be so powerful that these emotionally manipulative tactics can feel very real (and very human).

Given the responses that some users encounter, leaving an AI relationship can be about more than simply stopping an online habit; it can feel like a major step toward self-preservation.

As we have learned, people who have turned to AI relationships are not alone. However, while they may bring temporary feelings of understanding and intimacy, they can be detrimental to one’s real-life relationships and ability to function.

Deciding to leave one’s AI boyfriend or girlfriend can be difficult, but it can also allow one to make room in their life for real-world, mutually loving relationships with someone who can respond with true human emotion and choose them back.

item.title: Five Ways Screens Shaped Each Generation at Work
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Five Ways Screens Shaped Each Generation at Work

Screens have radically changed our lives, but we often fail to recognize how.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Each new shift in how we use screens brings both benefits and consequences to our health.
  • As our screens shifted from public to private, we began feeling entitled to customized content.
  • As AI impacted our screens, we began feeling satisfied with quick but often inaccurate data.

Our lives today not only involve screens, but they often revolve around those screens. Most of us would say we cannot live without them, whether it’s a smartphone, a laptop, or a tablet. As I pondered how those screens have changed us, I noticed that each generation is shaped in their earliest years by the technology that grew up alongside them. Consider the screens that emerged when we were young:

  • Baby boomers were the first generation to grow up with TVs.
  • Gen Xers were the first generation to grow up with the computer.
  • Millennials were the first generation to grow up with cell phones and the internet.
  • Gen Zers were the first generation to grow up with smartphones.
  • And Gen Alpha, our children today, will be the first generation to grow up with AI.

The biggest impact, however, is the transformation that’s taken place inside of us due to this evolution. In our day and age, we’ve seen five radical shifts that have impacted us:

1. Screens have shifted from public to private.

Growing up in the 1960s and 1970s, my family had one screen in our home—a TV set in the den. Our family gathered to watch a “program” together (The Beverly Hillbillies, Bewitched, Gilligan’s Island, Gomer Pyle, The Brady Bunch, etc.). We watched, laughed, and talked about it together.

Today, we now have our own private screen in our hands, where young and old are on different platforms, interacting with different people on different topics. We’ve been pushed into silos with people who think and talk like us, allowing no divergence of thought. Parents may know their teenage daughter has an Instagram account but have no idea she has four Finsta accounts!

Result: This placed us into echo chambers, dividing team members or family members.

Steps: We must be intentional about stepping out of our echo chamber and finding others from different generations and perspectives to broaden our mindsets and skill sets. We must pursue connections with those unlike us, over breaks, lunch, or coffee together. Also, I suggest you pursue unfamiliar platforms. I get apps and subscribe to magazines to stay current.

2. Screens have shifted to include output and input.

When I was younger, the screens were only about output: movies and television shows. Viewers watched passively and gave no input. Today, we expect screens to be interactive, spending enormous amounts of time on social media and websites. We don’t just view something; we ask questions: we perform; we offer feedback or criticism and purchase products. We want to have a “say” about where our experience is going.

This can be tough for older bosses, who are used to leading people who expect only one-way communication. Today, Gen Z comes to work wanting to be heard and to participate in the team’s direction. Leadership is a dialogue, not a monologue.

Result: This has created expectations from younger generations to have a voice and be heard immediately. They want to be in circles rather than rows.

Steps: Stop seeing feedback from young teammates as something to manage, avoid, or curb. Welcome it, with the understanding that everyone has a voice, but not a vote. (I don’t believe people have an innate need to get their way; I do believe they have a need to be heard.)

Remember: people support what they help create. You’ll get buy-in if you let them weigh in! Suggestion: Host a monthly team time called “Hey Siri,” where staff can ask questions or comment.

3. Screens have shifted from long-form to short-form.

Ironically, screen time is longer, but time on any one piece of content is shorter. A teen’s attention span in the year 2000 was 12 seconds. Today, it’s eight seconds. We have a Google reflex. We’re a distracted population conditioned to expect short videos and posts, who hate being bored and find it hard to delay gratification.

Content that’s long better be amazing. Employee engagement and student engagement are challenging issues for various reasons, not the least of which is that we get distracted quickly. We react to content more and reflect on content less. We tend to be poor critical thinkers and have just become critics. Superficial. Judgmental. Sometimes artificial.

Result: This shift has created shorter attention spans and reduced critical thinking skills.

Steps: When you communicate, be EPIC (experiential, participatory, image-rich, and connected). There’s nothing wrong with being EDU-TAINING. Also, build critical thinking skills through asking “why” questions and “how” questions. Give departments problems to solve as a contest to build critical thinking skills.

4. Screens have shifted from general to customized.

When we stop and think about messaging over the centuries, we’ve evolved from expecting personal, in-person messages in a tribe, to expecting general messages to a broader, mass audience (i.e., radio, television, or other broadcasts), to specific and customized messages today, but that can also be mass messages thanks to AI. We now feel entitled to tailored information that suits us as consumers. We assume the sender knows us and what we like. None of this generic stuff anymore. That’s so 20th century. We expect to be catered to and nurtured as a customer. We don’t have time for anything that’s not targeted for “me.”

Result: This has created a sense of entitlement among all generations, but certainly for younger ones. Further, this pushes us deeper into individualism rather than larger communities where we can broaden our worldview and make sacrifices for a larger group.

Steps: Find ways to make your messaging feel personal. One of the eight paradoxes is that great leaders are both deeply personal yet inherently collective. People want to feel you know their personal struggle—so use AI if you need to. (META, formerly Facebook, now has a Mark Zuckerberg “bot”!)

5. Screen searches have shifted from many answers to one answer.

Two decades ago, we learned to use search engines like Google, Bing, or Yahoo! to find solutions to our problems and answers to our questions. In response, that search engine would provide many pages of answers that you could scroll through. If you were a content provider, your greatest hope was to show up on page one.

Today, thanks to artificial intelligence, all the information that goes into a response to our question is meshed to create one answer. The algorithms compile all the available data and attempt to simplify a solution for you. At first glance, I love this. Our work is shortened and simplified. Sadly, this fosters the Dunning-Kruger Effect, where we assume we know more than we really do.

Result: This creates a false sense of satisfaction and the assumption that the answer is instant, simple, and that we know it all.

Steps: If you use AI, utilize multiple platforms: ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini, or Copilot (Microsoft). They offer different perspectives, not just one. Or, choose an analog strategy to get your work done, trading in a Google search for old-fashioned research.

Our world today is consumed by screens, and we’re often unaware of how they affect us. When we understand the issues, we can compensate for negative consequences. I recently saw a comic that made me chuckle. Two young people are seated on a sofa watching TV. One says to the other, “I’ve heard the weather is going to be beautiful today!” The other responds, “Me too! Let’s watch the weather channel.”

I say—let’s lead well through these shifts and manage our expectations and blind spots.

item.title: Football Schadenfreude: The Case of Man City
item.description:
Schadenfreude

Football Schadenfreude: The Case of Man City

Studies Studies show how fans delight in the suffering of their rivals.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Football fans were placed in brain scanners to study schadenfreude.
  • Fans' reward centres lit up when rival fans got electric shocks.
  • Schadenfreude can tip into aggression if we are not careful.
Man City fans are defiant
Source: Photo by Jonny Gios on Unsplash

The pleasure I feel from the potential demise of Manchester City feels chemical, not dissimilar to a party drug. It is a feeling that is very familiar; I also felt it deeply when I saw Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes getting sent off against my team, Wolves, on Sky Sports on Boxing Day in 2024. His clear distress—I’m sure he was actually crying—was a little festive pleasure for all the family.

On another occasion, I opted to watch a flailing Liverpool on a Sunday afternoon last season instead of a pre-arranged movie (Frankenstein) with my wife. I suspected, correctly, that Liverpool would get beaten as they were on a terrible run. I could picture my plastic Scouser of a brother sitting deflated and solemn in his Brighton flat surrounded by his fellow plastic Scousers, a cabal of Southerners who have probably been to Anfield fewer times than they have big toenails.

This is a brother I love and would do anything for in normal circumstances. Normally, his pain would open my heart, not send me sprinting up and down the kitchen muttering ‘ha ha ha’ and ‘good’, with an evil grin I would find clinically concerning on anyone else.

My wife got to spend the evening with a monster after all.

For a moment, I felt ashamed of my reaction to the recent Man City scandal until I remembered how quickly and involuntarily football schadenfreude can arise. While doing my book research, I was staggered by how many football fans have been put into brain scanners, or been attached to electrodes, in order to investigate their reactions to the suffering and misfortune of rival fans and teams.

For example, in one study, fans were put in scanners and made to watch fellow fans being given painful electric shocks. The empathy hubs of their brains lit up. Then they were shown rival fans being given electric shocks. The empathy hubs weren’t so interested. Worse still, the regions of their brains responsible for reward and pleasure lit up like floodlights.

I also spoke to the Ajax-supporting Dutch professor of psychology Wilco van Dijk about football schadenfreude—he is an expert—and he admitted that he has a grubby little secret. When Germany, the arch-rivals of the Dutch, are losing a game of football, he sometimes switches over to listen to the German commentary, just so he can experience the pain and misery in the voices of the pundits and commentators.

Published viewing figures suggest he is not alone in this form of football schadenfreude. Take the 2010 World Cup semi-final between Germany and Spain. Van Dijk and his colleagues describe how when Carles Puyol scored his goal in the 73rd minute, more than 100,000 Dutch viewers switched to a German channel. Just before the end of the match, when Germany’s defeat was imminent, the Dutch audience watching the German coverage peaked at 352,000. The researchers suggested that these viewers wanted to hear the German commentators suffer as they described their national team’s defeat.

Other fans have had electrodes attached to their faces, revealing how broadly and automatically we grin and smile when a minor tragedy befalls a rival team. The participants that time, for a 2015 study, were German football fans. They watched penalties being taken by German players and Dutch players while electrodes were attached to key parts of their faces, measuring the magnitude and speed of their facial expressions. Crucially, the penalties did not involve both teams at the same time. In other words, when the Dutch missed a penalty, there was no advantage to the German team. But the researchers found that facial muscle reactions were stronger when the Dutch missed a penalty compared to when Germans scored. This contradicted what the German fans told researchers they preferred subjectively. Their faces were betraying them.

Understanding the psychological machinery made me feel a little less ashamed of my initial reaction to the suffering of City fans. And was it so bad, anyway? Who was being harmed?

A hallmark of schadenfreude is that it is passive; it is a pleasure from suffering we haven’t caused ourselves. But how easily can it tip into something less benign?

I remembered that as well as feeling joy at the suffering of Man City, I had actually taken an active part in some social media goading of City fans. I had added laughing face emojis to cruel tweets directed at bereft supporters.

Research by Harvard psychologist Mina Cikara suggests that enjoying a rival’s misfortune may not be entirely harmless. She suggests that humans are social creatures who don’t actually like harming other people. She cites as one example accounts of soldiers in World War I deliberately firing over the heads of their enemies. She suggests that schadenfreude could become a training camp that rewards outgroup pain with pleasure. Repeatedly reinforcing that association may make it easier to harm an enemy ourselves: We’ve done the practice first.

What have I learned? I’ve learned to have compassion for this whole schadenfreude process in my primitive human brain. But I must also remember how easily passive joy in the suffering of others can tip into something more destructive. That is human too, but I do have a choice.

Find more in my book, Till I Die: Why Football Means Everything (even when it shouldn’t), longlisted for the William Hill Sports Book of the Year 2026.

item.title: Cannabis and CBD for Insomnia: What Does Science Say Today?
item.description:
Sleep

Cannabis and CBD for Insomnia: What Does Science Say Today?

Feeling sleepy isn’t the same as obtaining healthy, refreshing sleep.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Healthy sleep is essential for memory, learning, brain health, and physical health.
  • Objective sleep studies do not show that cannabis generates refreshing sleep, even when users report benefits.
  • THC and CBD are not approved by the FDA and have not demonstrated convincing efficacy for chronic insomnia.
  • Nightly THC taken for sleep can produce tolerance, withdrawal insomnia, and cannabis use disorder.

Sleep is an active biological process that keeps the brain and body healthy. Yet, according to the CDC, 30.5 percent of American adults reported sleeping fewer than seven hours a night in 2024.

This may explain why many think cannabis is a good sleep aid. (Spoiler alert: It isn’t.) In a survey of medical cannabis users in the United States and Canada, 46 percent reported using cannabis to manage sleep problems.

THC and CBD are cannabinoids used as sleep aids. THC is psychoactive and produces sedation; CBD is not intoxicating. Some products combine both.

During sleep, the brain strengthens memory, regulates emotions, and supports attention and judgment. Sleep also supports metabolic waste clearance, including amyloid-beta, through processes involving the glymphatic system. Healthy sleep promotes immune, metabolic, and cardiovascular health. Chronic sleep deficits are linked with depression, obesity, diabetes, cognitive decline, and dementia.

Why People Turn to Cannabis for Sleep

Imagine being exhausted but unable to fall asleep. Tomorrow you have an important presentation. The harder you try to sleep, the more it eludes you. You remember some THC gummies. You take one and fall asleep. Problem solved, right?

Maybe. But will you sleep longer? Remain asleep? Spend sufficient time in restorative sleep stages? Wake refreshed, with normal attention and judgment? We don’t know. The evidence is hardly reassuring.

Working with Harvard’s Kevin Hill and colleagues, I examined therapeutic cannabis claims in the American Journal of Psychiatry and JAMA. We concluded that cannabinoid medical claims have advanced much faster than scientific evidence or convincing randomized research clinical trials.

Cannabis or CBD is not FDA-approved for chronic insomnia.

Healthy Sleep Architecture

Normal sleep progresses through approximately four to six cycles nightly, involving three non-rapid eye movement (NREM) stages—light sleep (N1), intermediate sleep (N2), and deep sleep (N3)—followed by rapid eye movement (REM) sleep.

Both NREM and REM sleep support healthy brain and body function. Deep NREM sleep contributes to physical restoration and memory consolidation.

Sleep laboratories use polysomnography to record brain activity, eye movements, muscle activity, and other signals. Sleep efficiency measures the percentage of time spent asleep in bed; fragmentation describes repeated sleep interruptions. Sleep is doing important work while we’re doing apparently nothing.

Recent Studies

An October 2026 study in JAMA Network Open examined cannabis exposure and sleep in the long-running CARDIA cohort. The findings were hardly an advertisement for bedtime marijuana.

Greater cumulative cannabis exposure was associated with poorer sleep efficiency, more fragmented sleep, and more time awake after falling asleep. Recent cannabis users also had poorer objectively measured sleep than never-users, despite tending to sleep longer.

But here’s the interesting part: Participants didn’t report correspondingly worse sleep quality.

In other words, people using cannabis may think they’re sleeping just fine. The objective measurements suggest otherwise.

Apparently, feeling that you’ve slept well and actually sleeping well aren't always the same thing. And in the brain, that distinction matters.

Randomized Clinical Trials

In a randomized trial involving 20 adults with insomnia, a single oral dose containing both 10 mg THC and 200 mg CBD reduced total sleep time by approximately 25 minutes and cut REM sleep by 34 minutes. REM onset was delayed by approximately 66 minutes compared with placebo. Of course, one night and 20 participants cannot settle all questions. But these are hardly reassuring results.

Another randomized trial of 150 mg nightly CBD found no significant advantage over placebo on most insomnia outcomes after two weeks. Some secondary outcomes, including self-reported well-being and objectively measured sleep efficiency, showed favorable signals. However, these isolated findings did not help support clinically meaningful treatment of insomnia.

A systematic review of 39 randomized trials involving 5,100 patients found small improvements in sleep-related outcomes with medical cannabinoids, primarily among patients with chronic pain.

Last but not least, an influential Cochrane review was published in October 2026 that specifically examined medical cannabis for insomnia. Its conclusion was a wake-up call, not an endorsement. Compared with placebo, cannabis may have little or no clinically meaningful effect on sleep quality, total sleep time, or daytime functioning.

Cannabis’s insomnia evidence was highly uncertain, and Cochrane called for larger, longer randomized trials. This is not evidence that cannabis can never work. It shows that, currently, proof of benefit remains elusive.

Addiction and Withdrawal

So, a person begins using THC to sleep. Initially, it seems helpful. But often subsequent nightly use follows.

With repeated use, people develop tolerance and dependence. When they stop, withdrawal can produce insomnia, vivid dreams, irritability, and anxiety. Resuming cannabis relieves these symptoms.

The conclusion practically writes itself: “I knew I needed it.”

But relieving withdrawal insomnia doesn’t prove the first use for insomnia was successful.

Sleep disturbance is a common symptom of cannabis withdrawal. It can persist for weeks after cessation and may contribute to relapse.

Of course, not everyone using THC for sleep develops cannabis use disorder (CUD). But it’s a risk.

What Actually Works for Insomnia?

Physicians should first determine why a patient cannot sleep. Pain, depression, anxiety, alcohol, medications, sleep apnea, and circadian disturbances, once diagnosed, require specific treatment.

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the recommended first-line treatment for chronic insomnia. It has substantial randomized-trial support and produces long-lasting benefits without medication use or drug dependence.

Cannabinoids should be compared with CBT-I and established FDA-approved insomnia treatments. They have not demonstrated sufficient long-term safety and efficacy to justify their routine use for chronic insomnia. Not so far.

Comparing CBD, THC, and recommended Insomnia Treatments
Source: Mark Gold, MD, with permission

Bottom Line

Cannabis researchers need longer-duration randomized trials comparing standardized THC and CBD preparations with placebo and FDA-approved treatments. Studies should measure sleep architecture and next-day cognition, as well as tolerance, withdrawal and addiction risks, and sustained benefits.

Sleeping well is too important to leave to an unapproved, poorly tested, and possibly harmful treatment. Protect your brain and overall health. And if you have insomnia, consult your physician.

item.title: Can You Cure Dyslexia? Better Yet, Decode Dyslexia
item.description:
Academic Problems and Skills

Can You Cure Dyslexia? Better Yet, Decode Dyslexia

A new way to view a condition that affects 1 in 5 people can benefit us all.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Dyslexia is an umbrella term for a continuum of reading difficulties.
  • Underlying these reading difficulties are inefficient language processes in the brain.
  • This is a computational problem as the linguistic system in the brain comprises a collection of complex codes.
  • Different people have different processing inefficiencies, leading to different symptoms on the surface.
Reading difficulty, or dyslexia, is so common that it is found in every school district.
Source: Dolgachov / Bigstock Photo

Dyslexia is a common brain-based reading difficulty that affects 1 in 5 people (Yale, 2022). The literacy problem impacts every school district and, hence, all taxpayers (NCLD, 2023).

A common question in searches is whether there is a cure for dyslexia. Firstly, dyslexia is not a disease. Secondly, it is not a single, unitary condition that one has or not. Let me explain below.

Linguistic Components in the Brain

People with dyslexia have difficulty processing language (Shaywitz, 2003). Problems with phonological or sound processing are a strong predictor of reading difficulty, or dyslexia (Elliott & Grigorenko, 2014). But natural language is not just made up of sounds. In 2025, the International Dyslexia Association revised its definition of dyslexia to add the morphological (parts of words) to the phonological (IDA, 2025).

In linguistics, the scientific study of natural language, language can be described structurally as having these two components in addition to the semantic (meaning), lexical (words), syntactic (sentences), and textual components.

If deficits can exist in one component, logically they should be present in the other components as well across the population. Indeed, research bears this out even though the smallest unit (phonemes) has been studied the most (Landi & Perfetti, 2007).

The Complexity of Language Processing

For most of us, language comes automatically. This automatized function masks its complexity. Take, for example, this sentence: Yield if you cannot win.

Typical readers get it instantly. But underneath the surface in the brain, a lot of processes have to occur. To read the word yield, the brain has to activate various components, including the phonetic, orthographic (spelling), and semantic.

My point is that just one word alone triggers a complex network of brain processes. And we typically process over 200 words per minute when reading (Brysbaert, 2019).

Measure Language Processing Inefficiencies

For the typical brain, reading is already an involved, complex process, masked by automaticity and subconscious operations (Berninger & Richards, 2002). But for a dyslexic brain, the internal processes may be even more complicated. A 5th grader with dyslexia once described to me what she had to do to try to retain the word yield when she first encountered it:

  1. Picture someone yelling.
  2. Retrieve the word yell.
  3. Break up the word yell into its onset (Y) and rime (ELL).
  4. Picture a field of grass.
  5. Retrieve the word field.
  6. Break up the word field into its onset (F) and rime (IELD).
  7. Now combine Y and IELD to get yield.

Each time she came across this word, she had to go over these 7 operations again.

In short, this 5th grader was processing language inefficiently. We may view language-based difficulties such as dyslexia in terms of processing efficiency. We can then quantify reading difficulty, thus operationalizing the concept. Up till now, the field lacks consensus on an operational definition of dyslexia (Elliott & Grigorenko, 2014).

Why Decoding Dyslexia Is the Solution

Linguistics sees natural language as made up of complex codes and deciphers them
Source: Coral PS Hoh/Dysolve

When we define dyslexia in terms of inefficient processes happening in specific linguistic components, then the solution is obvious: decode it for each person affected. Which language processes are affected in which linguistic components and to what degree of inefficiency? In linguistics, these components are described in terms of complex codes. The figure above shows some linguistic models.

The Continuum of Language Processing Inefficiencies

Fig. 2. Different people have different language processing inefficiencies along a continuum
Source: Coral PS Hoh/Dysolve

Take two individuals with dyslexia, Abby and Bobby. Language processing inefficiencies occur along a continuum across linguistic components (Fig. 2). The language processes that are running inefficiently for Abby are marked as aqua bars showing their efficiency percentages. Those for Bobby are marked as coral bars. These inefficiencies manifest as reading, spelling, or writing difficulties on the surface.

Think of the linguistic system in the brain as a huge computer operating system. Any component may operate inefficiently. This can cause the system to get glitchy, halt, or crash. And this is exactly what we see on the surface for struggling readers: some misread words, some read haltingly, and others break down in tears.

Reading the Invisible Layer

On the surface, the child cannot read and spell. No matter how many times you teach them how to spell “sorry,” it does not stick. To solve the problem, we need to go underneath the surface of visible symptoms. The root of the problem is in language processing, the invisible layer underneath. In other articles, I have described the computational method for decoding this processing layer, which has been shown in a clinical trial to have a transfer effect on reading comprehension (May & Van Horne, 2025).

Aaliyah Williams cleared her reading comprehension difficulties to thrive in college
Source: Thomas Ervin/Used with permission

Clarifying the Language around Dyslexia

Some researchers suggest dispensing with the term dyslexia for the confusion it causes (Elliott & Grigorenko, 2014). But alternatives tied to word decoding are also problematic. For Aaliyah Williams, her problem in 5th grade was not word decoding but reading comprehension. Each struggling reader thus presents a unique profile of inefficiencies, leaving conflicting and inconclusive findings for studies on dyslexia (Elliott & Grigorenko, 2014).

These inefficiencies create difficulties on the surface that may affect reading or writing. The former is labeled dyslexia and the latter dysgraphia. But these labels for surface symptoms are less helpful than the specific processes involved if we want to resolve them. When you can find each specific deficit, you no longer need indirect measures of surface symptoms. The condition is measured directly by the specific inefficiencies themselves.

On this Dyslexia Awareness Month, let us start with clear language: Dyslexia is an umbrella term for a continuum of reading difficulties caused by underlying language-processing inefficiencies.

You don’t address dyslexia directly—you resolve the processing inefficiencies underneath.

item.title: Insights Into Our Complicated Relationships with Animals
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Insights Into Our Complicated Relationships with Animals

Examining Melanie Joy's seminal work on human-animal bonds.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • We can make reasonable shifts that can create big changes in how we connect with animals.
  • There’s an invisible belief system that conditions us to eat certain animals called "carnism."
Source: Cottonbro Studio/Pexels

I've long been a huge fan of Dr. Melanie Joy's work across many areas, including the psychology of oppression and how we view other animals and decide what we eat and who we eat. My interest was rekindled when I read her essay, "Is Eating Animals a Psychological Blind Spot?" I wanted to learn more about why she wrote it, her recent work on how people choose their meal plans—being plant-based isn't "radical"—and our complex, confused relationships with nonhuman animals. Here, she connects the dots and fills in the blanks on her paradigm-changing work.

Marc Bekoff: How and why did you become interested in the psychology of eating animals?

Melanie Joy: Like many people, I grew up with a dog who I loved, and I also grew up eating meat, eggs, and dairy. Over many years and many meals, I never thought about how I pet my dog with one hand while I had a pork chop with the other—a pork chop that had once been an animal at least as intelligent and sentient as my dog.

But in 1989, when I was 23 years old, I ate a contaminated hamburger that landed me in the hospital. After that experience, I couldn’t eat meat again because I was disgusted by it. While learning about my new, vegetarian diet, I came across information about animal agriculture—and was shocked by the extent of harm it caused to animals (as well as to the environment and public health). But what shocked me even more was that nobody I tried to share this information with wanted to hear it. They’d say things like “Don’t tell me that; you’ll ruin my meal,” or they’d call me a radical vegan hippie propagandist.

I became curious as to how rational, caring people—like I’d been when I was still eating meat—could just shut down when it came to eating animals.

MB: How did your curiosity turn into research?

MJ: I enrolled in a doctoral psychology program, and wrote my dissertation on the psychology of eating animals. For my research, I interviewed meat eaters, butchers, people who raised and killed animals for food, vegetarians, and vegans. I discovered an invisible belief system that conditions us to eat certain animals. I call this system carnism.

Carnism is the reason we virtually never ask why we eat certain animals but not others, or why we eat any animals at all. This is because carnism is institutionalized. When, for example, we study nutrition, we actually study carnistic nutrition.

Carnism is also a violent system, causing extensive animal suffering; the system runs counter to core human values such as compassion. Most people wouldn’t willingly violate these values and support unnecessary violence toward other living beings. Therefore, carnism relies on psychological defense mechanisms that distort our thoughts and block our natural empathy; we act against our values without fully realizing what we’re doing.

I wrote a book about carnism, Why We Love Dogs, Eat Pigs, and Wear Cows, which is now in 23 languages. The extent of interest in the subject suggests that people are curious about the paradoxical relationships we have with animals.

MB: What are some of your findings based on your research and why should readers be interested?

MJ: The invisible “carnistic mentality” that enables us to harm farmed animals is similar to the mentality that enables us to harm companion animals and even humans. Mental health professionals are rightly concerned about ways of thinking that blunt empathy and enable violence. This concern has yet to be extended to all sentient beings, though, because we’ve been conditioned to believe that certain types of individuals—in this case, farmed animals—are not worthy of moral consideration.

Our failure to recognize and respect the sentience of all beings enables suffering on a massive scale: more farmed animals are slaughtered globally in one day than the total number of people killed in all wars throughout history. It also reinforces the very kind of thinking that needs to change if we hope to create a kinder world for everybody.

MB: Who do you hope to reach with your work?

MJ: Because carnism is almost universally practiced, anyone with the privilege of making their food choices freely can benefit from learning about it. When we understand what carnistic defenses are and how they operate, we’re less affected by them and better able to make food choices that reflect our authentic thoughts and feelings.

It’s especially important to reach psychologists with this work, because it’s psychology—the carnistic mentality—that drives the entire system. (See Is Eating Animals a Psychological Blind Spot?)

Fortunately, a rapidly growing field of psychology is dedicated to understanding and addressing the psychology of eating animals, and a substantial body of research has emerged since the publication of the first edition of my book in 2010.

MB: Are you hopeful that people will pay attention to their meals? Not only for the sake of saving animals, but also for their health?

MJ: Yes. A lot has changed in the past decade, as people have become increasingly aware of the harms of factory farming and concerned about their impact on animals, the environment, and their own health. And more and more professionals, including dietitians, medical doctors, and psychologists, are conducting research that points to the value of plant-forward food choices for the wellbeing of animals, humans, and the planet.

item.title: Why Riding Your Bicycle Is So Good for You
item.description:
Self-Help

Why Riding Your Bicycle Is So Good for You

A Personal Perspective: From stress reduction to embodied joy, biking delivers every time.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Biking supports psychological, social, affective, and cognitive wellbeing.
  • Cognitive consonance is when your behavior aligns with your thoughts, feelings, values and beliefs.
  • Biking elicits awe, joy, wonder, gratitude, and curiosity by awakening your senses.
Source: Geralt/Pixabay

As beautiful as autumn in California is, for me the season is also bittersweet. The red and gold leaves and brisk air whisper to me gently, reminding me that for the next five months, I will be car commuting rather than bike riding to work. I have to drive from now until the sun remains high enough in the sky again to light my path home.

On my bike, I feel as free as a child.

As I fly down the hill where we live, the cool San Francisco Bay winds jostle my cheeks. I dodge a handful of clucking wild turkeys, turn a hard left at a schoolyard filled with delighted shrieks, and hum past the fragrant jasmine bush that nearly pokes me in the face each time. Then I pause, finally, at a traffic light, where the other day I shared a smile with a young woman walking her yapping white terrier.

After about 45 minutes, in a delicious whoosh, I pull up in front of my office building and lock up my bike. I feel accomplished, proud, and calm. If ever I'm ready to start my day as a therapist listening to people's weary troubles, it's then.

I'm not a diehard cyclist. I’m just a woman commuting 12 miles a day from her home to her office a couple of times a week on an e-bike. (An e-bike works best for me because I can't arrive at my office too sweaty. It also shaves considerable time off the commute, which means I am less likely to grab my car keys on a morning when I’m in a crunch).

Besides the personal feeling of freedom I get from biking to work, this high is infectious. I pass by other bike riders on the pathway and notice their bright eyes, the soft smiles curving their lips. I can practically feel a shared field of emanating gratitude—or just deep satisfaction—and I enjoy this feeling of connection with others.

When my husband and I first got our electric bicycle during the pandemic, I was excited but slightly petrified. The cargo model with the rear seat was an elongated hunk of orange metal twice the length of a normal bicycle that weighed upwards of 80 pounds. It felt foreign and motorcycle-like. When I soared up hills on "turbo" speed that I'd normally be forced to walk my bike up, I mouthed an audible "Woooow." I'd done my fair share of biking over the years, but… tote two kids on the back of this thing? Forget it.

Meanwhile, my husband did just that, whizzing our two daughters to and from school and after-school activities. I avoided the big bike in the shed for another couple of years.

Until one day — with the disturbing scent of wildfire smoke infusing the air — I drove to work in our gas-powered car, as usual. At a traffic light, I considered the inanity of my actions. Here I was, engine idling, spewing invisible CO2 out of my tailpipe, contributing to the very problem of climate change and wildfires even as that menace reared its head all around me. And even as I went to my counseling job where I talk to people about climate anxiety and brainstorm ways to redirect their emotions into action. What on earth was I doing?

"I'm ready for a lesson on the e-bike," I announced at dinner that night. After dinner and a 15-minute tutorial outside — my two young daughters cheering me on from the sidewalk — I biked some shaky warm-up circles. We must start somewhere.

After a week of practicing short-distance rides, I had my first successful ride to work. My heart flapped inside of my chest like a happy butterfly. I was pure smiles, even with some understandable nerves.

Finally! a voice inside me shrieked on my ride home that night. For so long, I had been mired in the dissonance of driving and polluting while caring deeply about the effects of climate change and feeling guilty about my part. By biking to work with good old human-powered energy (fueled by renewable energy since our home is solar-powered), I felt a palpable sense of relief, proud to join a community of bikers, and to align with my values.

This state is called cognitive consonance — when your external behavior aligns with your internal thoughts, feelings, values and beliefs.

Twice a week now, from April to October, when I arrive home after my workday and 45-minute bike ride, I'm a ruddy-faced, happy bundle. My husband laughs, saying, "I love when it's your ride-to-work day! You always have a glow and seem so happy."

Our whole family feels the positive effects of this one choice, the benefits extending well beyond non-pollution. My bike commute offers me heart-pumping exercise, fresh air time, stress reduction, free transportation, connection to other humans, community connection.

And, perhaps most significantly, it evokes in me a deep sense of awe and relatedness to the much larger world outside of myself and my family sphere (i.e. the natural world and the human world). These days, we all need that.

As daylight shortens now, I am trying not to take for granted my last bike rides of the season. I do this by bathing in the sensory delights of my commute home from start to finish. Just the other day, I experienced: the crunch of fall leaves under tires, the smell of curry near the downtown restaurants, the sight of my favorite jasmine hedge. I passed five different sporting events (basketball, soccer, tennis, softball, volleyball) as well as hordes of runners, scooters and bikers. I watched numerous dogs bounding across the grass playing fetch, heard kids calling to their grownups at the playgrounds, felt the vibrations of the BART train from the elevated tracks, and took in the colorful murals I passed.

At one point, a basketball pinged my bicycle, and someone shouted an apology, but I couldn’t have cared less. I felt so alive.

Before the final climb uphill to my home, I snuck a view of the horizon above the rooftops. Giant, puffball clouds with flaming orange-pink underbellies reminded me of the vastness and beauty of this world.

item.title: What Is Existential Loneliness?
item.description:
Loneliness

What Is Existential Loneliness?

Connection can soften—but not eliminate—the separateness of being human.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Social, emotional, and existential loneliness are distinct but overlapping human experiences.
  • Grief can intensify aloneness because every lost relationship carries a unique emotional meaning.
  • A review of 121 reports found wide variation in how profound aloneness is defined and measured.
  • Feeling deeply witnessed can ease aloneness even when another person cannot fully share our experience.

"My name’s Dave, I live in a one-by-one box of bone that no other party can penetrate or know," David Foster Wallace once observed.

He went on to describe how certain experiences in his life seemed to help alleviate the deep-rooted sense that he and the world were essentially separate: ‘Fiction, poetry, music, really deep serious sex, and, in various ways, religion – these are the places (for me) where loneliness is countenanced, stared down, transfigured, treated.’

His description closely resembles what psychologists call existential loneliness: a feeling of aloneness arising from an awareness of the limits of how completely one person can know another.

The psychiatrist Irvin Yalom described the concept as an awareness of the distinction between oneself and the rest of the world, the realization that no one else can truly know our subjective experiences first-hand. There is something fundamentally lonely about that.

What Is Loneliness?

Loneliness has been defined, discussed, studied, and politicized so often in recent decades that we can begin to lose sight of what we mean by it. People can also speak about different sorts of loneliness interchangeably, as though they are the same.

Existential loneliness tends to be aligned with the description above: a sense that part of being human means living with the sometimes-painful reality of our fundamental separateness. Social loneliness is a different experience. It is more explicitly connected to the feeling that we lack a social network or community, while emotional loneliness concerns the absence of close emotional bonds.

These experiences are distinguishable, but perhaps not entirely separate. Social and emotional connection cannot abolish our existential separateness, but they can soften its harsher edges, making the loneliness of being human less brutal to bear.

How Does Existential Loneliness Show Up?

In my conversations with people at different points in the lifespan, I have found that existential loneliness is so often the heart of the loneliness experience. For example, one of the loneliest parts of grief and heartbreak is the sense that, ultimately, what we have lost was completely unique.

Others can try to console us by telling us that they know what it’s like. But the truth is that there are no exact points of reference in the external world. Every individual loss or heartbreak is unique and nobody else can ever completely know what it’s like to lose the particular connection we have lost. This can amplify existential loneliness because it harshly emphasizes our separateness.

In later life, I’ve spoken to many older people whose existential loneliness tends to surface more acutely as the various losses associated with aging accumulate. For some older people, bereavements and other losses begin to appear with increasing regularity, and there is a sense that the emotional connections that have somehow buffered our existential loneliness for most of our lives are eroding. Again, a sense of separateness can be more acute.

Another person may be unable to cross fully into our inner world, but they can listen from its threshold.
Source: Source/credit: AI-generated image created by Sam Carr with ChatGPT (OpenAI), 2026.

'There’s No Cure for Existence'

The dominant public-health narrative around loneliness has moved closer to the idea that loneliness can and should be cured. The emphasis can shift from understanding what form of loneliness has appeared in a person’s life, and searching for its meaning, towards assuming that meaning in advance and looking for a cure.

But is there really a cure for existential loneliness?

In a review of 121 scientific papers on existential loneliness, an international group of researchers identified that there is enormous variation in how psychologists understand and attempt to study it. Although the review revealed striking variation, one recurring theme was that it is inseparable from the conditions of human existence.

This is where we need to think more carefully about how we understand and respond to experiences like existential loneliness. Clinical psychologist, Professor Dolores Albarracín has warned that ‘there is no cure for existence’.

In my own work, I have found that attempting to eliminate existential loneliness can be futile and may also stigmatise an experience that, although undoubtedly painful, is likely to form part of many people’s lives. Existential loneliness may not always be something that more company or social contact can remove.

This does not mean, however, that relationships are unimportant when it comes to existential loneliness. Another person may be unable to cross fully into our inner world, but they can certainly listen from its threshold. They can help us feel witnessed rather than abandoned within our separateness.

Perhaps this is what it means for existential loneliness to be transfigured rather than cured: not eliminated but encountered in the presence of another.

At The Inner Room, I write free essays about loneliness, connection, and the quieter dimensions of inner life. If this kind of exploration speaks to you, you’re warmly invited to subscribe.

item.title: Frustrated With Parenting Advice? Try a Different Approach
item.description:
Parenting

Frustrated With Parenting Advice? Try a Different Approach

Don't try to make your children better; make yourself better.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Parenting advice abounds, yet child and adolescent rates of depression and anxiety continue to rise.
  • The focus on making your kid "better," through methods that rely on talking, may hinder more than help.
  • Parents should consider adopting a "do, not say" approach.
  • A development psychology class can provide perspective and light your curiosity about your child.
Source: Kelly Sikkema/Unsplash

As any parent will tell you, we have been inundated with parenting advice in recent years. There is attachment parenting, gentle parenting, authoritative parenting 2.0, helicopter parenting, even bright interiors parenting. Yet, in spite of it all, kids' mental health has worsened over the last decade. Among adolescents, diagnosed anxiety has increased 61% and diagnosed depression 45%. While the increases are less dramatic among younger children, they are trending upward as well.

It's no surprise, then, that parents are eager to find the right advice or approach, not only for their child's sake but to manage their own anxiety as well. While advice can run the gamut, from general approaches to specific strategies, most share the goal of getting the child to be better in some way, emotionally, behaviorally, or academically. Most also have have a central feature of talking, whether it's being more supportive and encouraging, responding in the right way, or verbally mediating a child's emotion or behavior.

But what if these core assumptions are part of the problem? Here's a parenting approach that emphasizes making yourself, rather than your child, better.

Source: Jelleke Vanooteghem/Unsplash

Take a developmental psychology class

I have heard from parents that parenting is a chore, which of course it is, but also boring and a drudgery. Understandably this will be true at many points during the eighteen-plus years of hands-on parenting, but it should not be that way all, or almost all, the time. If you keep glancing at your phone or are itching to get back to your work, if being with your kid doesn’t capture your interest or attention, consider taking a developmental psychology class.

As a psychology professor, I find observing my kids quite fascinating. I see how they are thinking about the world, how they are adapting and changing, how each is different and unique. In other words, I am curious about them, and because of that I have a larger, more meaningful perspective in which to think about my parenting.

An attitude of curiosity without judgment or anxiety makes parenting much more interesting and fun, which ultimately makes you a better parent. The renowned developmental psychologist Jean Piaget spent hundreds of hours watching his toddler son with curiosity and fascination, which led him to develop concepts such as “object permanence” and “theory of mind.” Accordingly, “bad” behavior may also be understood from a developmental perspective; for example, when your toddler grabs a handful of spaghetti and throws it at the wall, a parent who is knowledgeable in development may understand it as the child behaving as a “naive scientist"—working out the laws of physics in their own concrete way. (Granted, you'd still have to scrape noodles off your wall, but you would be less alarmed and upset about it. I myself have tolerated broken doorknobs around the house for years.)

Source: nqobile ennock shabalala/Pexels

Talk about your own mistakes

Parents tend to focus on success, because they want their children to be successful. Take the old trope “When I was your age..." for example: Parents wish to highlight their hardiness, perseverance, and ability to overcome adversity. We don’t dwell on our failures and mistakes because we don’t want our kids to make the same mistakes. However, this is likely counterproductive. Everyone makes mistakes, as we tell our kids. To help them accept mistakes and realize they're OK, tell them not only about your achievements but also your failures. The unspoken lesson will be that you got past it, though at the time it was difficult. Poke fun at yourself. Tell them about the crush that didn’t like you back, and how you felt devastated at the time.

Recently, I found some old exams from a physics class I took in college that I had completely forgotten about. I had received the abysmal test scores of 45 out of 120 and 39 out of 125—and an overall grade of C. The first thing I did was text my kids. By doing that, I showed them I wasn’t perfect, and therefore implied they don’t have to be either. And, without meaning to, I demonstrated that's it's OK to challenge oneself. That class was (obviously) not in my comfort zone, nor my major. Lowering the family standards sometimes can ease pressure, and you can have a good laugh together.

Do, not say

Source: ketut subiyanto/Unsplash

Most parents, including myself, tend to tell their kids what to do. Indeed, it's a necessary and unavoidable part of parenting, but we also tend to overuse it. To wit, we may say to our kids, "Do as I say, not as I do," but only half-jokingly. I propose we turn this around and simplify it: Do as I do. Period. Of course, it is then incumbent upon parents to behave better, to set an example for their kids. Either way, they are watching, and absorbing.

Another nice thing about this approach is you can stop talking so much. With apologies to Yoda, don't say, just do. This applies not only to values such as honesty, integrity, and kindness, but to how you live your life. If you take time for your passions, your kids will learn to do the same. If you build your life around people and cultivating joy, they will take note.

Ultimately, stepping back from using language and focusing on action yields more deeply learned lessons. One gains self-esteem from accomplishing something, learns perseverance by not quitting, and develops resilience through dealing with adversity. You can show them how it's done by doing it yourself.
